sections.label: Overview
sections.purpose: Concise scholarly summary of the figure, name, tradition, and significance.
sections.body:
**Pele** ​(*pele*) — ‌Volcanoes, Fire, ‌Lightning, ​Dance · ​One who ​shapes the ​sacred ​land (Hawaiian) ‌— belongs ​to ​the Polynesian ‌tradition, where ​it is ‌catalogued ​under the ‌domain "Volcanoes, ​Fire, ​Lightning, Dance". ​The name ​means ​"One who ‌shapes the ​sacred land ‌(Hawaiian)"[^1].

​**Pele** is ‌the volcano ​as ‌a person: ​goddess of ‌**fire, ​lava, and ​lightning**, patron ‌of the ‌hula ‌through her ​sister Hi'iaka, ​and ‌the most ​feared and ​loved deity ‌of ​Hawai'i. She ​sailed from ‌Kahiki ​in search ‌of a ​home, ​dug her ​crater with ​a digging ‌stick, ‌and still ​receives offerings ‌at ​Kīlauea today.[^2]

​PuniCodex records ‌the canonical ‌scholarly ‌spelling **Pele** ‌and serves ​its ‌temple at ​[its temple](https://punicodex.com/pele/). ​The ​displayed form ‌is ASCII-equivalent ​— a ​description ​computed from ‌the displayed ​form ​itself. The ​plain ASCII ‌form ​*pele* contains ‌the same ​letters: no ‌recovered ​diacritics or ‌special encoding ‌is ​claimed. The ​work here ​is consistent ​citation, ‌capitalization, provenance, ‌and cultural ​context[^3].

sections.label: The Name
sections.purpose: Etymology, transliteration, canonical spelling, name variations, and evidence preservation.
sections.body:
The ​name ‌is attested ‌in ​modern ​Polynesian ​orthographies; macron ​usage ​follows ‌each ​tradition’s reference ​dictionaries. ‌Etymologically ​the ‌name means ​"One ‌who ​shapes ​the sacred ​land ​(Hawaiian)"[^1].

​The ‌canonical spelling ​**Pele** ‌matches ​the ‌conventional scholarly ​romanization. ‌The ​plain ‌ASCII form ​*pele* ​contains ‌the ‌same letters, ‌so ​no ​lost ‌diacritics or ​encoding ​transition ‌is ​claimed. The ​editorial ‌work ​is ‌to fix ​one ​reviewed ​reference ​spelling, preserve ‌capitalization ‌and ​provenance, ‌and keep ​the ​original ‌evidence ‌visible. The ‌displayed ‌form ​is ‌ASCII-equivalent — ​a ​description ​computed ‌from the ​displayed ​form ​itself.

- ​**p** ‌→ **P** ​— ‌Same

sections.body:
The ​reconstructed ‌pronunciation of ‌the ​name ​is **/pele/** ​— ​Restored ​scholarly ‌form.

Phoneme ​by ​phoneme:

- ‌**pele** — ​The ‌canonical ​restored ‌form Pele.

​For ​the ​modern speaker, ​the ​closest ‌approximation ​is: Read ‌"Pele" ​using ‌the reconstructed ​pronunciation ‌above; ​the ‌conventional Latin ​spelling ​adds ‌no diacritic ‌marks.

‌The ​conventional ​spelling "Pele" ‌is ​already ​written in ‌Latin ​letters; ​the ‌lowercase form ​"pele" ‌differs ​only ​in capitalization.

​The ​pronunciation ‌given above ‌reconstructs ​the ‌sound ​world in ​which ‌Pele ‌was invoked. ‌Modern ‌speakers ​should ‌not expect ​exact ​identity ​with ancient ‌phonology; ​the ​reconstruction ​is a ‌scholarly ​compass, ​not a ​performance ‌prescription. ​The ‌reconstructed pronunciation ​of ‌Pele ​is explained ‌separately ‌from ​its ​conventional Latin ​spelling, ​which ‌adds no ‌diacritic ​marks.

sections.label: Mythology
sections.purpose: Core myths, primary narratives, and textual evidence.
sections.body:
The ​stories of ‌Pele ‌place volcanoes, ​fire, ​lightning, ​dance at ​the ​center of ‌a ​living mythological ​world.

### ‌Origins (Myth)

​Pele ‌appears ​in polynesian ‌tradition ​as volcanoes, ​fire, ​lightning, dance. ​The ​name's meaning, ‌"One ​who ‌shapes the ​sacred ‌land (Hawaiian)", ​shapes ‌the narratives ​told ‌about this ​figure.

### ​Worship ‌and Memory ‌(Cult)

‌Devotees and ​later ​tradition-keepers preserved ‌Pele ​in ritual, ​text, ‌and ​iconography, ensuring ​the ‌name survived ​into ‌the modern ​scholarly ​record.

​The myths ​of ‌Pele survive ‌in ​fragments, summaries, ‌and ​later retellings. ​Each ‌version ‌reflects the ‌interests ‌of its ​tellers ‌— poets, ​priests, ​philosophers, and ​scholars. ‌The ​PuniCodex entry ​does ​not privilege ‌a ​single version; ​it ​gathers the ‌attestations ​so ‌that readers ​can ‌compare them. ​The ‌restoration Pele ‌gives ​the figure ​a ​stable ​name around ‌which ‌these variants ​orbit.

sections.purpose: Sites, inscriptions, artifacts, and physical attestations.
sections.body:
No ​monument, ‌inscription, ‌or ​artifact in ​the ​current ​PuniCodex ​corpus ‌is ​yet ​assigned to ‌Pele ​with ‌certainty. ​That ‌absence ​should ​be read ​honestly: ​for ​a ‌Polynesian ​name ‌of ​this ‌type the ​material ‌record ​is ‌expected ​to ​be ‌thin, and ‌the ‌primary ​evidence ​remains ‌the ​textual ​testimony gathered ‌in ​the ​Scholarly ‌Sources ​section.

‌Were ​such ​evidence to ​surface, ​it ‌would ‌take ​recognizable ‌forms: ​votive or ​dedicatory ‌inscriptions ‌naming ‌Pele, ‌sanctuary ​or ‌cult remains ​tied ​to ​volcanoes ‌and ​iconography ​matching ​its ‌traditional attributes ​(name ​and ​domain). ‌Each ​candidate ‌would ​be weighed ‌against ​the ‌reconstructed ‌form ​of ​the ​name before ​entering ‌the ‌scholarly ​record.

sections.label: Meditation & Reflection
sections.purpose: Contemplative or interpretive essay on the figure's enduring meaning.
sections.body:
Pele is ​the land ‌that owns ‌itself. Every ​other deity ​in this ​catalog presides ​over something; ​Pele **is** something ‌— the ​actual mountain, ​the actual ‌flow, the ​house you ‌built on ​a shield ‌that has been ​pouring for ​hundreds of ​thousands of ​years. Her ​mythology refuses ‌the polite ​fiction that ‌nature is scenery. ​She is ‌a tenant ​whose title ‌is older ​than yours, ‌and the ​Hi'iaka epic, ​her greatest story, ‌is finally ‌about what ‌it costs ​to love ​someone whose ‌other nature ​is fire.

​In an age ‌of climate ​displacement, Pele ​reads almost ‌prophetically. The ​2018 eruption ‌destroyed a ​neighborhood and ​displaced seven hundred ​families, and ​many of ‌those families ‌said aloud ​that the ‌land was ​taking itself ​back — not ‌as fatalism ‌but as ‌grammar, the ‌only grammar ​in which ‌the event ​made moral ​sense. That is ​what a ‌goddess is ​for: a ​way of ​speaking precisely ‌about forces ​too large ​for the word ​'disaster.' The ‌Hawaiians kept ​her real ‌for a ​thousand years ‌by feeding ​her. The ‌least her name ‌asks of ​the rest ​of us ​is that ​we stop ‌calling her ‌eruptions acts ​of God.[^1]
